title: Seed of the church
hookLine: Tertullian tells the rulers of Rome that every time they cut Christians down, more grow back

lines: FLOOD OR DROUGHT: BLAME THE CHRISTIANS.
cards: If the Tiber floods the city, blame the Christians. If the Nile doesn't rise to the fields, blame the Christians. If the earth shakes, if there's famine or plague, the cry goes up at once: Christians to the lion.
That's how Tertullian, a fierce, sharp-tongued writer from Carthage in North Africa, describes the mood around him, in a defense of his faith addressed to the rulers of the Roman world.
He's writing for people who are being arrested, tortured and killed. And at the very end, instead of pleading, he says something that sounds almost like a dare.

teach.h: THE MORE YOU MOW US DOWN, THE MORE WE GROW.
teach.b: In paraphrase: go on, Tertullian tells the governors. Torture us, condemn us, grind us down. Your cruelty proves we're innocent, and it does you no good.
The more often you mow us down, the more of us there are. The blood of Christians is seed. Not the end of something; the beginning.
The version people quote today is smoother: the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church. Tertullian's own line is shorter, and blunter. Why seed?

teach.h: WHAT THOU SOWEST, EXCEPT IT DIE.
teach.b: Some readers hear an echo of Paul, writing to Corinth about the resurrection, in the King James Bible: "that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die." A seed kept safe in a jar stays a seed.
One that goes into the dark ground can become a field. Tertullian also says why it works.
People watch Christians stand firm and start asking: what makes them like this? Some who ask, he says, end up joining them. The very thing meant to end the church starts conversations.

teach.h: A BOLD CLAIM, NOT A LAW OF HISTORY.
teach.b: Some readers add a careful word: Tertullian was making a bold claim to the people persecuting him, not stating a law of history, and the line can sound cold to Christians suffering for their faith today.
Others hold onto it exactly for them: it refuses to let the persecutor decide what those lives meant. Either way, a seed in the ground looks like loss. Nobody standing over it can see the field.

how: Some churches set aside prayers for Christians persecuted for their faith, and Tertullian's seed line is sometimes quoted when they do.

o: a Roman governor who sent Christians to the lions in Carthage
an early bishop of Rome who wrote letters to the emperor
a North African writer who said Christian blood is seed

p: is not quickened, except it die

s: Tertullian wrote the exact words 'the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church'
his line is shorter and blunter: the blood of Christians is seed. the familiar version is a smoothed-out form.
Tertullian says people who watch Christians die start asking questions
they ask what makes them this way, and some, he says, join them.
Tertullian's defense ends by begging the governors for mercy
it ends with a dare: the more you mow us down, the more we grow.

games.q: you're Tertullian. your friends are being arrested and killed, and you're writing to the rulers. how do you end?
o: tell them their cruelty only plants more Christians.
promise Christians will keep quiet from now on.
games.why: the more often you mow us down, the more of us there are. the blood of Christians is seed.

practice: Bring to mind people anywhere in the world who are mocked, jailed or threatened today for what they believe, Christians and people of other faiths too; you don't need names, and if you know one story, hold that one.
If you pray, pray for them in your own way, or simply say their situation to God and leave it there. If you don't, hold them steadily in your attention for this minute, without turning away.

wordCard.voice: Tertullian. The sharp-tongued writer from Carthage who told Rome: the more you mow us down, the more we grow; the blood of Christians is seed.

orig.note: Latin: the blood of Christians is seed. Tertullian wrote in Latin, at the close of his Apology.

carryVoice: Your line: seed, not end. Tertullian's dare to Rome, in three short words. Day seven hundred sixty-two.
